processing: Typical of raw pu-erh from Menghai: sun-dried green leaf (maocha), sold loose or pressed, with no ripe-style piling.
harvest_season: As usual across Menghai, spring picking is the prized one.
appearance_dry: As with Hekai old-tree tea, fairly slim, long dark leaves.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear gold when young, as with young raw pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Typical of raw pu-erh, olive-green leaves softening as they steep.
taste_profile: Little is documented about Banpen on its own. Hekai teas in general are described as high-scented and sweet with some bitterness and astringency, less bitter than Lao Man'e and less forceful than Lao Banzhang.

brewing.notes: Standard young raw pu-erh approach; short first steeps keep the astringency in check, as is usual for Hekai teas.

vintage_note: Like other raw pu-erh, it is sold by harvest year, usually spring material pressed the same year, then drunk young or stored. It is a small village name usually met in single-origin pressings; check the village and year, and do not assume a connection with Banzhang from the similar sound.
description:
Banpen, also written Bangpen, is an old village among the Hekai tea villages near Menghun in Menghai County. It is listed with Guangbie, Manlong, Mannong and Manmai as part of the Hekai group.

Hekai is known for one of the larger stretches of old tea garden in the area. The leaf is made the usual raw pu-erh way, with sun-drying and no ripe-style piling.

Little is documented about how Banpen itself tastes. Hekai as a whole is described as high-scented and sweet with some bitterness, gentler than the Bulang heavyweights, so that is a fair starting expectation.

Despite the similar sound, this is not Banzhang, which belongs to a different area. Ask a seller which village the leaf came from and which year it was picked.
history: Little is documented about when tea began at Banpen or who brought it to notice. It appears in lists of Hekai's old villages, and its name is known mainly through the modern interest in single-village raw pu-erh.
